content: The pelvic cavity is a body cavity that is enclosed by the bony structures of the pelvis. It primarily houses the reproductive organs, the urinary bladder, and the rectum. The boundaries of the pelvic cavity are defined as follows: Greater and Lesser Pelvis: The lesser pelvis, also referred to as the true pelvis, includes only the structures located below the pelvic brim. For instance, the pelvic splanchnic nerves, which originate from spinal levels S2 to S4, are located within the true pelvis. In contrast, the femoral nerve, which arises from spinal levels L2 to L4, is situated in the false pelvis, also known as the greater pelvis. The pelvic cavity is supported and stabilized by various ligaments and supplied by specific arteries and nerves: Ligaments: These provide structural support to the pelvic organs and maintain the integrity of the pelvic cavity. Arteries: The primary arterial supply to the pelvic cavity includes: The internal iliac artery The median sacral artery The ovarian artery (in females) Nerves: The innervation of the pelvic cavity is provided by: The sacral plexus The splanchnic nerves Additional anatomical details include: The articulations of the pelvis, as seen from an anterior view. The arterial supply to the pelvis. Dissections of the lateral pelvic wall, which reveal the sacral and pudendal plexuses. The sacral plexus on the right side, which is a key component of the pelvic nerve network.
